lens: Brand and art direction — does this read as a real, desirable clothing brand's site, or as a decorated template? Judged on: art-directed vs decorated; whether the site respects a washed, muted, restrained product or fights it; whether TIME is an intelligent structural idea or a costume; and ruthless application of the vibe-coded tells checklist.

strengths: Time as DATELINE is the only genuinely non-decorative reading of the theme in the set. It is how a magazine handles time — issue numbers and datelines — and it gives the 10px wide-tracked mono a real job (a label attached to an object) rather than a decorative eyebrow. Delete every hourglass from this site and six of its seven time expressions survive. That is the test, and only this concept passes it cleanly.

SPREAD 03 — THE PLATE. A 78svh full-bleed image with no type, no product, no UI, hard-cut in and hard-cut out, carrying one 10px dateline in the corner. A screen with nothing on it is the single hardest thing to get past a client and the clearest proof of an art director in the room. Neither other concept has the nerve.
Navy #141B2C as INK on paper instead of black. That is a fashion-house decision, it costs nothing, and it is the kind of thing a template never does.

The off-grid discipline is real, not claimed: 83/100 aspect derived from an actual flat-lay crop (the ALD 69/50 move), images bleeding off the left viewport edge on three of seven spreads, and column 8 of twelve left deliberately empty so the gap IS the composition. Vertical rhythm set per spread by the image, not a global py-24.

The crop language (backs turned, cropped at jaw, mid-stride, hands given a job, two front-on faces on the entire site, both small in frame at 85mm) correctly identifies that the category's real film language and the AI model's failure modes point the same direction — and then commits to it as a policy rather than an excuse.

The refusal list is exhaustive and each refusal costs something: no ticking-clock cursor, no live-time header, no hourglass spinner, no sand canvas, no Roman numerals in UI, no tessellated monogram behind text, no wordmark stretched across the hero. It also correctly bans its own most obvious move — 'OUR TIME' as an H1 over a centred hero.

The narrative arc is load-bearing on the CORRECTED name specifically: EARN EVERY SECOND at the top, TIME WON'T WAIT in the middle, OUR TIME spent exactly once at the bottom after the sand. That arc only became available when the name changed from OVERTIME, which is the strongest available proof the design was made for this brand and not retrofitted.

The palette arithmetic dictates the shot list, not just the CSS: washed grey at 1.84:1 on paper and washed black 8 points off the ground force a per-colourway `bg` field in the catalogue. A production constraint discovered in the colour, not patched afterwards.
weaknesses: The hero garment is shown at full editorial scale on spread 01 and then the site spends spread 02 on a six-up shorts run. That is the right order, but time-to-product is a full screen of video with zero affordances on it. For Palace that is confidence; for a brand whose own footer says EST. 2026, it is a gamble.

The one sequence is pure atmosphere. It is a beautiful Blender hourglass that resolves into a typographic payoff line — it never lands on a garment. Concept 2's match cut is strictly better craft on the same asset.

Söhne is Aimé Leon Dore's own face, chosen while citing Aimé Leon Dore as the reference. The proposal argues the differentiation is 'in the system, not in owning a rare face' — that is a rationalisation. Wearing the reference brand's typeface is a soft originality failure.

Chronological-default collection sort is a pose on a 31-colourway catalogue. The shopper wants 'shorts, medium, cream'. The concept admits this and then leans the whole recovery on a filter bar it also calls chrome.

Thirteen pages plus a 260vh pinned sequence is a lot of surface to keep at this standard. The concept's own risk note is correct: it fails in revision, not in design, and there is no slack to absorb one bad client note.

Almost no commerce warmth anywhere. No fit guidance, no garment-dye disclosure, no returns reassurance designed into a page — all of it is pushed into PDP accordions. For a heavyweight oversized washed product sold online to strangers, that is a real hole that Concept 3 fills brilliantly.
fatal_flaws: The datelines are fiction. 'DROP 01 — PHOTOGRAPHED 09.26 / NORTH TRACK, 19:40 BST' describes an AI image made at an invented location, and the site's whole time system is built on those captions. A magazine dateline works because it is a record; a fabricated one is a costume with better manners than an hourglass spinner, but a costume. Worse, it sits on the same page as the footer line 'CAMPAIGN IMAGERY CREATED WITH AI' — the site contradicts itself in 10px mono. This is not unfixable, and it must be fixed before build: real render dates, real drop dates, real dispatch times, and no invented place names.

strengths: The MATCH CUT is the best single piece of craft in the entire set. Frame 123 of the hourglass sequence and the still of the back-print photographed at the same crop height, same key-light angle, same subject scale, so crossing the pin boundary reads as a cut, not a transition — and explicitly rejecting a morph because 'a cut is more premium than a transition'. That is a film editor's decision applied to a scroll boundary. Steal it.

Redaction 35 — a serif drawn in graded states of degradation — used on exactly one line, on one section, and nowhere else on the site. A face chosen because its drawing register IS the distressed-engraving register of the back-print, then deployed with real scarcity. That is typographic art direction, not a font pairing.

Neue Haas Grotesk in two OPTICAL sizes (Display 55/65 + Text 55/75) with the explicit reasoning that this gives two registers without importing a second personality — and the explicit refusal of Söhne, Akkurat and Favorit because the category has already claimed them. This is the only concept that notices it should not wear its reference brands' typefaces.

It actually computes the contrast rather than eyeballing it: #171717 on #0F0F0F is 1.07:1, and the fix is applied at GENERATION time (SH-05 prompted onto a warm sand backdrop) rather than patched in CSS. The other two state the risk; this one does the arithmetic and moves it upstream.

'The glass empties, and the glass arrives' — the nav going solid over the moving canvas and cross-fading to glass at the pin release makes the performance mitigation and the concept's punctuation the same decision. Genuinely elegant.

The design-changed-because-of-the-checklist section is the most honest of the three: it names five places where a tell overruled the designer's first instinct, including killing its own scroll-indicator idea.
weaknesses: The lap splits (00:00 / 02:00 / 02:41 / 04:15 / 06:00 / 24:00) are section numbers in fancy dress. The concept knows they are one step from a scroll-progress bar and its mitigation is a code comment. And 24:00 for the footer 'because the brand owns 24/7' is a pun, which is always the point where a theme becomes a costume.

Renaming functional UI in brand voice: sold out becomes TIME'S UP, restock becomes BACK ON THE CLOCK. Corteiz — the reference for anti-template attitude — says 'Sold Out'. Cute state names on size chips are the exact register the rest of the proposal is trying to avoid.

Time-to-product is 260vh of falling sand, then one silent full-screen garment photograph with no price, then a grid. On an unknown label with zero existing demand that is two full screens of atmosphere before anything is purchasable.

It leans hardest on the one asset nobody can guarantee. The proposal says so plainly: 'this direction has a single point of failure and this is it.' If the Blender hourglass looks like a stock 3D asset, the entire homepage is a gimmick.
Naming the sections after timecodes in the deliverable is internal cleverness leaking into the page — the reader sees 02:41 on a rule above a shorts grid and has to be told what it means.

One model for DROP 001 versus two elsewhere means the collective 'OUR' — which the corrections explicitly called out as the brand's register — is carried by no image at all. Concept 1 and 3 both shoot a crew frame; this one does not.
fatal_flaws: The spine of the concept is a 260vh scroll-scrubbed hourglass draining. The teardown's own cliché ranking puts the hourglass and the clock face at the top of what everyone builds for a time-themed site, and this proposal bans the hourglass spinner, the sand-particle canvas and the SVG clock face — then makes the largest possible literal hourglass the front door of the brand. The back-print justification is real and it is the best defence available, but it does not clear it: enacting the metaphor at full screen for two and a half viewport heights is the cliché with a bigger budget. Concept 1 spends the same asset far more intelligently — cropped so the top bulb runs off frame, filling rather than draining, held back as a payoff at the END rather than used as the entrance.

strengths: 'SOLD OUT — 23:14, SUN 12 OCT' is the best single idea in all three documents. Stock written as a timestamp is free, it is true, it is the most persuasive social proof a small brand has, and it is the one place in the set where the time theme does commercial work instead of being worn. Nothing else in the category does this.

The archive as an accruing ledger of windows that opened and closed — closed drops kept live at their own handles, every sell-out timestamped, the counter replaced by 'CLOSED 23:00, SUN 12 OCT · 7 PIECES · 4 SOLD OUT'. It costs nothing to build, it only makes sense for a brand called OUR TIME, and it gets better every drop.

The FIT & CARE band is the most convincing writing anywhere in the set: 'Garment-dyed and washed. Expect up to 3% shrinkage and slight colour variation between pieces. That is the process, not a fault.' Plus the real model line (6'1"/185cm, chest 38", wearing M) and a real measurement table. Specific, slightly unflattering honesty is something no generated site produces, and it is exactly what a heavyweight washed product sold to strangers needs.
No red anywhere on an e-commerce site. Genuinely uncomfortable, and the single clearest proof the palette came off the garments rather than out of a framework.

2px gutters on the product rail — a contact sheet, not a card wall — plus the grid bleeding 40px past its container so the third column is cropped by the viewport. Two small, correct, art-directed moves.
The drop as a RANGE (11:00 FRI → 23:00 SUN) rather than a date, counting to the close rather than the open. Corteiz's inversion, correctly understood.

Putting the counter and the bag in the glass pill makes the one piece of chrome carry the one number that matters. It is the tightest marriage of the client's liquid-glass request to the brand concept in any of the three.
weaknesses: It reads as an excellent shop rather than a desirable brand. Hero → 4-up quick-add rail → sequence → colour bar → trust band → payoff is Gymshark's rhythm, not Aimé Leon Dore's. It will convert better and it will look less wanted, and for an aspirational washed-premium label that is the wrong trade at launch.

The mobile pill morphing into [S][M][L][XL] · ADD is strong UX and weak brand — a persistent bottom bar with size chips is what every Shopify theme's sticky ATC looks like. The proposal pre-empts tell #36 by arguing it is the only defensible version of the pattern; the defence is thin.

It designs for seven SKUs and explicitly refuses a filter panel, when the corrections confirm seven garment types and roughly thirty colourways and demand a genuine collection architecture. The colour-bar pattern does not extend to seven garment types, so the homepage needs a re-layout the moment the confirmed range lands. Concept 1 built that architecture; this one flagged it and built the smaller thing anyway.

'1,284 ON THE LIST' is a stats band with one number (tell #29). The concept guards it with 'a real number or nothing' — which is the right rule — but a follower count on the page is still the move a generated site makes.

The one emotional beat (OUR TIME over the crew shot) is one screen out of eleven, arriving after the commerce. That ordering is defended as 'what makes it land', and commercially it is right, but it leaves the brand's own name as a closing caption on a site that has spent the preceding hour selling.
fatal_flaws: A live countdown pinned permanently into the nav chrome, on every screen of the site including the cart, is the thing the teardown specifically names as the failure mode: 'Scarcity that's always on isn't scarcity; it's a Shopify app.' Corteiz's timer is a temporary top bar during a genuine closing window, not furniture. A launch brand with no demand yet running a permanent visible countdown reads as pressure, and pressure is the cheapest register in streetwear.

The hero sequence is the most technically fragile asset proposed by anyone: sand animated as a luma matte inside the print region of a single AI still, displaced by a Depth Anything map of the tee so the fill line follows the fabric folds, across 96 frames. If that lands at 80% it does not read as art direction, it reads as a filter applied to a nice photograph — and unlike the other two concepts' Blender renders, there is no deterministic path to the result. The risks section calls this 'the hardest asset to make' and still understates it.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: The match cut. End the pinned hourglass sequence by cutting — not transitioning — into a full-bleed still of the navy tee's back print, framed at identical crop height, identical key-light angle and identical subject scale, so the pin boundary reads as an edit. No morph, no crossfade.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: THE SLOW HAND's single structural weakness is that its one expensive moment resolves into a typographic payoff and never touches a garment. The match cut makes the site's climax land on the product, which is the difference between a concept and an atmosphere. It also costs nothing extra — it is a framing constraint on a Blender camera and a shot-list note, enforced by compositing the two frames side by side before rendering.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: Drop Söhne. Use two OPTICAL sizes of one grotesque — Neue Haas Grotesk Display (55/65) for display, Neue Haas Grotesk Text (55/75) for body — plus one mono.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: THE SLOW HAND cites Aimé Leon Dore as the reference and then proposes shipping ALD's actual typeface, arguing the differentiation is in the system. That is the same logic as shipping the most-starred glass component. Two optical cuts of one family gives the identical two-register discipline without wearing the reference brand's face, and it sidesteps Akkurat (Cole Buxton) and Favorit (SSENSE) at the same time.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: One degraded serif — Redaction 35 — used on exactly one line, on one section, and nowhere else. Set the single line of brand copy on the Story page in it.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: THE SLOW HAND bans serifs outright, which is a defensible rule that also removes its only chance of a note. A face whose drawing IS the distressed-engraving register of the hourglass back-print, deployed once with total scarcity, is not a font pairing — it is the same restraint logic the concept already applies to the wordmark (twice on the whole site) extended to one more mark. It is free and OFL.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: Compute the washed-black contrast properly (#171717 on #0F0F0F is 1.07:1, not 'eight luminance points') and enforce the fix at GENERATION time — the washed-black colourway is prompted onto a warm sand backdrop in the image prompt, not corrected in CSS afterwards.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: THE SLOW HAND has the right instinct and stops one step short, treating it as a shot-list rule and a catalogue `bg` field. Moving it into the prompt means the asset can never arrive wrong, which matters far more than a CMS field when the asset costs money and QA attention rather than API spend.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: Stock written as a timestamp: 'SOLD OUT — 23:14, SUN 12 OCT' on the card and the PDP, instead of a grey badge.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: This is the best idea in the entire set and it belongs in the winner, not the loser. It is the purest expression of THE SLOW HAND's own thesis — time as the filing system, dates as metadata — applied to the one place the concept currently defaults to a plain 'SOLD OUT'. It is free, it is true, and it is the most persuasive social proof a launch brand has.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: The archive: closed drops stay live at their own handles with every size struck, every sell-out timestamped, and the counter replaced by 'CLOSED 23:00, SUN 12 OCT · 7 PIECES · 4 SOLD OUT'. After four drops, /archive is a ledger of windows that opened and closed.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: This retroactively JUSTIFIES THE SLOW HAND's most contested decision — chronological-first collection IA. Right now a ledger-by-default sort is a pose that fights a shopper who wants cream shorts in a medium. With an accruing archive behind it, the time-first order stops being an affectation and becomes the front end of a real record. It is also free: it is the collection page with a closed state.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: The drop expressed as a range — 'DROP 01 · 11:00 FRI → 23:00 SUN' — rather than a date, and the FIT & CARE band's garment-dye honesty copy plus the real model-measurements line, designed as a full section rather than buried in a PDP accordion.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: The range is a better dateline than a date and slots straight into the existing metadata layer. The fit/care band fixes THE SLOW HAND's one commercial hole: it has no page anywhere that reassures a stranger buying a £68 oversized washed tee sight-unseen. 'Expect up to 3% shrinkage and slight colour variation between pieces. That is the process, not a fault' is the most brand-true sentence written by any of the three, and hiding sizing behind a tap is a measured returns cost.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: No red anywhere on the site — sold-out, errors and low-stock all resolved in washed grey, a strike, and an inline word — and 2px gutters on the product rail rather than 24px.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: Both are small, both are uncomfortable, and both are the kind of decision that proves the palette and the grid came from the garments rather than from a framework. THE SLOW HAND's 24px-gutter ledger grid reads as a card wall; at 2px it reads as a contact sheet, which is the correct register for a page whose whole argument is that it is a printed document.

verdict:
THE SLOW HAND wins, and it wins on the only question that matters through this lens: which of these could plausibly be a real clothing brand's site rather than a very well-argued website about a clothing brand.

It is the only one where the time idea survives deletion of the props. Strip every hourglass and clock from all three and Concept 2 loses its spine entirely, Concept 3 keeps two good ideas (the timestamp, the archive), and Concept 1 keeps six of seven — because it put time in the filing system rather than on the wall. Time as dateline, chronology as IA, dates attached to objects: that is how a magazine handles time, and it is the only reading in the set that is structural rather than illustrative. It also gives the brand's fragile thin wide-tracked treatment its correct and only home — a 10px mono label attached to a thing — which is the exact ALD inversion, tight and huge or tiny and tracked, never both.

And it is the only one with the nerve to put nothing on a screen. SPREAD 03 is 78svh of photograph with one caption in the corner and no purpose beyond confidence. That single decision tells me more about whether there is an art director in the room than any of the twelve pages of glass ladder in any of the three documents. Combined with the off-grid moves that actually cost something — 83/100 derived from a real crop, images bleeding off the viewport edge, column 8 of twelve left visibly empty, vertical rhythm set per spread by the image rather than by a global padding token — this is the only one of the three that would survive being printed.

Now the harsh part, and it applies to the winner too.

First: the datelines are fiction, and that is a real hit on the concept's own terms. 'NORTH TRACK, 19:40 BST' describes a place that does not exist, photographed on a date nothing happened, and then the footer discloses in the same 10px mono that the imagery was made with AI. The site contradicts itself. A magazine dateline is persuasive because it is a record; an invented one is a costume with better manners than a ticking-clock cursor, but it is still a costume, and it fails the proposal's own anti-tell #55 ('no real numbers, no real dates, no real place names') by answering it with counterfeits. Fix before build: real render dates, real drop windows, real dispatch times, and cut the invented place names. The system survives; only the fiction goes.

Second: Söhne is Aimé Leon Dore's typeface and this proposal cites Aimé Leon Dore as its model. 'The differentiation is in the system, not in owning a rare face' is a rationalisation, and it is the typographic equivalent of shipping the most-recognisable glass library. Take Concept 2's answer.

Third, and this is the one to say out loud to the client: restraint has no floor under it. This direction is only as good as its photography, it is being generated on a $15 pilot by a model with documented consistency weaknesses, and 'empty' is the single failure mode with no cheap fix — because every instinctive response to it (add a section, add copy, add cards) destroys the concept. The gate the proposal sets itself is correct and must be kept: OT-TEE-BACK and OT-PLATE-TRACK both clear client QA before a single line of layout is built.

On the losers. THE GLASS EMPTIES has the best individual craft in the set — the match cut, the one-use degraded serif, the two optical sizes, the properly computed contrast — and it spends all of it on the idea everyone has first. A 260vh scroll-scrubbed hourglass draining as the front door of the brand is the cliché with a bigger budget, and the proposal knows it, which is why it bans the hourglass spinner and the sand canvas on one page and then builds the largest possible hourglass on the next. Its lap splits are section numbers in fancy dress and '24:00' for the footer is a pun. Good hands, wrong idea.

THE COUNTER is the best business and the least desirable brand. It contains the single best idea anyone had — sold-out as a timestamp — and the most convincing copy, and it then arranges itself as a very good DTC activewear store: quick-add grid on beat two, a permanent countdown welded into the chrome of every page including the cart, and a sticky bottom size bar on mobile. A countdown that is always on is not scarcity, it is a Shopify app, and that is the teardown's own words. It also builds for seven SKUs when the corrections confirmed seven garment types and thirty colourways, which is a brief-compliance miss the winner does not make.

One observation across all three, which the client should hear: these are less different than they look. Same pill geometry, same three-tier glass ladder, same 0.78 scrim, same adaptive data-over flip, same specular sweep driven by scroll, same five-view character sheet, same one-key-light-no-fill rule, same Astro-plus-adapter stack. That is the research pack speaking with three accents. The real differentiation is in about four decisions per concept — and on that narrower comparison, THE SLOW HAND owns the best structural idea, THE GLASS EMPTIES owns the best single cut, and THE COUNTER owns the best sentence. Build the first, graft the other two, and do not let anyone add a section to it.
